sections.title: The Order of Conversion Like the Assembly at Mount Sinai
sections.html:
Just as the Children of Israel made a covenant with God at the Exodus from Egypt, and became His people when they received the Torah at the assembly at Mount Sinai, so the convert who enters Israel must undergo before the beit din a personal conversion process of making a covenant, which expresses his own Exodus from Egypt and his own assembly at Mount Sinai. As it is stated (Bamidbar 15:15): "As you are, so shall the convert be before the Lord." "'As you are' – like your forefathers: just as your forefathers entered the covenant only through circumcision, immersion and the sprinkling of blood (of a sacrifice), so too they (the converts) shall enter the covenant only through circumcision, immersion and the sprinkling of blood" (Keritot 9a).

At the time of the Exodus from Egypt, the Children of Israel underwent brit mila, as it is stated (Yehoshua 5:5): "For all the people who came out were circumcised," and regarding the brit mila that they underwent when they left Egypt it is stated (Yeḥezkel 16:6): "And I passed by you and saw you wallowing in your blood, and I said to you: In your blood, live; and I said to you: In your blood, live." Through brit mila Israel was set apart from the other nations to be the people of God, to bring His blessing to all the families of the earth, and to repair the world under the kingdom of the Almighty. This covenant is also a covenant of blood, which expresses the readiness of Israel to give their lives for their identity and destiny, as has become clear over the long history of the people of Israel, in which preserving Jewish identity has entailed self-sacrifice.

Before the giving of the Torah, God sent Moshe to Israel to ask them whether they wished to accept the Torah and the mitzvot. As it is stated (Shemot 24:3-8): "And Moshe came and told the people all the words of the Lord and all the ordinances," and the Sages explained that he reviewed before them the mitzvot they had already been commanded up to that time – the seven Noahide laws, Shabbat, honoring parents, the red heifer, and the laws between a person and his fellow (Rashi). Afterward he asked them whether they wished to accept the Torah and the mitzvot, "and all the people answered with one voice and said: All the words that the Lord has spoken we will do." Then Moshe wrote in a book the things that God had said to Israel up to that time. "And he took the book of the covenant and read it in the hearing of the people, and they said: All that the Lord has spoken we will do and we will hear." Similarly, in all generations, when a convert comes to convert, one must teach him some of the mitzvot before the conversion, so that he can decide whether he wishes to accept upon himself the entire Torah and the mitzvot.

In preparation for the assembly at Mount Sinai, all of Israel immersed in water, as it is stated (Shemot 19:10): "And sanctify them today and tomorrow, and let them wash their garments." The Sages learned that the instruction was that they sanctify themselves through immersion in preparation for the covenant they would make with God over all the words of the Torah, when the blood of the sacrifices would be sprinkled upon them (Mekhilta ibid.; Yevamot 46b; Keritot 9a). Through immersion in water, Israel was as if reborn in preparation for its great destiny: to be the people of God, to receive His Torah and to bring His blessing to the world.

In addition, in preparation for the assembly at Mount Sinai, Israel offered a sacrifice, and Moshe Rabbenu sprinkled its blood upon them in order to express their self-sacrifice for God and His Torah. Similarly, when the Temple stood, the convert had a mitzva to offer a sacrifice (below, halakha 14).

Thus we see that, like Israel, when a convert wishes to convert he must decide to leave Egypt: to shake off the wicked idolatrous conceptions that justify power at the expense of morality, to choose to prefer values and ideals over everyday needs and over natural family and social ties, and to decide to join the people of Israel and accept the Torah and the mitzvot in order to add life and blessing to the world. For men, the Exodus from Egypt is expressed through brit mila, and the entry into the people of Israel and the acceptance of the Torah through immersion, which is like being born anew. For women, everything is done through immersion.

sections.title: "Your People Shall Be My People, and Your God My God"
sections.html:
The beit din must examine the will of the convert – whether he truly identifies with Judaism and seeks to join the people of Israel in order to bring the word of God and His blessing to the world. In other words, the beit din must check whether the convert is ready to identify with the words of Ruth the convert, who said to Naomi: "Your people shall be my people, and your God my God" (Ruth 1:16). That is, to join the people of Israel, in the sense of "your people shall be my people," and to join the covenant of the people of Israel with God, in the sense of "and your God my God."

The Sages instructed (Yevamot 47a) that before the conversion one must ask the convert: "What have you seen that you have come to convert? Do you not know that Israel at this time is afflicted, oppressed, downtrodden and harassed, and sufferings come upon them?!" Today one should ask the convert: Why do you want to convert? Do you not know the great suffering of the people of Israel in this world – that during the long exile many nations persecuted us, and some even tried to annihilate us?! Not long ago the terrible Holocaust took place, and before that many severe pogroms. And even now there is antisemitism, and many wish to destroy us, and all this because we are Jews. And if you wish to rise in the levels of righteousness and morality, you are not obligated to convert, for any person from any nation can be righteous and one of the pious of the nations of the world, and can even merit divine inspiration. If the gentile gives up his request to convert, we part from him with respect.

If the convert stands firm in his desire to convert, one continues to clarify whether he wishes to enter the covenant of Israel with God and to accept upon himself the Torah and the mitzvot. For this purpose the Sages instructed (Yevamot 47a): "We inform him of some of the lighter mitzvot and some of the more stringent mitzvot, and we inform him of the sin of leket, shikheḥa and pe'a (gleanings, forgotten sheaves and the corner of the field) and the poor man's tithe. And we inform him of the punishment for the mitzvot; we say to him: Be aware that before you came to this state (of being a Jew), if you ate ḥelev (forbidden fat) you were not punishable by karet; if you desecrated Shabbat you were not punishable by stoning. But now, if you eat ḥelev you are punishable by karet; if you desecrate Shabbat you are punishable by stoning. And just as we inform him of the punishment for the mitzvot, so we inform him of their reward; we say to him: Be aware that the World to Come is made only for the righteous … And we do not overwhelm him, and we are not exacting with him."

That is, we teach the convert some of the mitzvot and inform him that if he transgresses them he will be punished for it by the hand of Heaven, and when the Sanhedrin exists, the beit din can even punish him for transgressions he commits deliberately and defiantly. We inform him of all this in order to examine whether he is truly ready to bear the great responsibility of accepting the Torah and the mitzvot, so that if he is not ready, he will be deterred and withdraw from the conversion process. However, on the other hand, the Sages instructed to explain to the convert the value of the mitzvot and their reward, in order to endear them to him. Likewise, they instructed to teach him before the conversion only "some of the lighter mitzvot and some of the more stringent mitzvot … and we do not overwhelm him, and we are not exacting with him." For even if his intention is for the sake of Heaven, there is concern that if he hears many stringent mitzvot all at once, he will be deterred and withdraw, for he will fear that he will not have the strength to learn all the mitzvot of the Torah and fulfill them (Baḥ 268:5, Shakh 5). But if he learns the mitzvot gradually, over time he will succeed in fulfilling them.

Among the mitzvot taught to the convert before his conversion are "gifts to the poor" – leket, shikheḥa and pe'a, which the owners of fields must leave for the poor – as well as the poor man's tithe, which must be set aside for the poor. This is because the mitzvot between a person and his fellow are a great principle in the Torah. In addition, the convert may be poor, and if he is taught these mitzvot, he will know how to support himself, just as Ruth the Moabite supported herself in her days of poverty by gathering the gifts to the poor. In addition, there was a concern that if the convert had a field and did not know that the poor have a right to take leket, shikheḥa and pe'a from it, he would think that they were stealing from him, and perhaps, to protect his property, he would rise up and kill them, as was accepted among the gentiles; and to prevent this they needed to teach him these laws (Yevamot 47b).

sections.title: The Study in Preparation for Conversion
sections.html:
In the past, the process of informing the convert of "some of the lighter mitzvot and some of the more stringent mitzvot" was short, and within a few days the beit din could convert the convert, and after the conversion the convert had to continue to study Torah and mitzvot and gradually grow accustomed to fulfilling them. However, nowadays the batei din usually require longer study before the conversion, and there are several reasons for this. First, the entire world has become more educated. Every profession today requires significant study; all the more so the study of Judaism, which includes beliefs and opinions, laws and customs, requires longer study today. Moreover, in our times people are exposed to opinions, religions, cultures and intellectual currents from all over the world, and accordingly, the study of the faith of Israel, its Torah and its mitzvot, must also be longer and more significant. In addition, in the past people were more accustomed to obeying the commandments of religion, and therefore it was possible to defer the study of the overwhelming majority of the mitzvot until after the conversion, on the assumption that every mitzva the convert would learn after the conversion he would grow accustomed to fulfilling. But today people are less accustomed to obeying the commandments of religion, and therefore the study in preparation for conversion must include more study of practical mitzvot and getting accustomed to fulfilling them, so that the one converting can examine whether he wishes to accept upon himself the mitzvot of the Torah.

In addition, many of those converting today are spouses of Jews or their descendants, and they seek to convert in order to strengthen their Jewish identity without knowing that Jewish identity includes a commitment to the mitzvot of the Torah. Therefore there is a need to devote more time to the study of the mitzvot.1

sections.title: Methods of Study in Preparation for Conversion
sections.html:
Sometimes, out of a desire to prepare those converting for a religious way of life, they are taught many details of the mitzvot and fine points of halakha, and thereby some converts are pushed away, deterred by the yoke of the mitzvot, which seems too heavy to them. However, the Sages already instructed (Yevamot 47a) that this should not be done, so as not to deter the convert and cause him to withdraw; rather, the convert should be taught before his conversion "some of the lighter mitzvot and some of the more stringent mitzvot … and we do not overwhelm him, and we are not exacting with him" (Baḥ 268:5, Shakh 5).

First of all, one must teach the one converting about the great destiny of the people of Israel, which rejects idolatry, whose purpose is to help a person satisfy his urges and achieve his goals, and instead believes in the Lord our God, faith in whom is meant to elevate a person to be good and moral, and to want to walk in the ways of God, to do righteousness and justice and to bring blessing to the world. As was said to Avraham our father when he was commanded to go up to the Land and to found the people of Israel (Bereishit 12:1-3): "And the Lord said to Avram: Go forth from your land, and from your birthplace, and from your father's house, to the land that I will show you. And I will make of you a great nation, and I will bless you and make your name great, and you shall be a blessing. And I will bless those who bless you, and the one who curses you I will curse, and in you shall all the families of the earth be blessed." And as the Torah explains why God chose Avraham to found the people of Israel and designated him to be a partner in the process of repairing the world, as it is stated (ibid. 18:18-19): "And Avraham shall surely become a great and mighty nation, and all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in him. For I have known him, so that he will command his children and his household after him to keep the way of the Lord, to do righteousness and justice."

Included in this, one must teach the convert about the period when we were slaves in Egypt, and that God took us out from there with signs and wonders and chose us to be His treasured people, in order to reveal to the world the value of freedom, to always remember the suffering of slaves and other unfortunate people, and to take care to honor them and do good to them. Following from this, the study in preparation for conversion should place central emphasis on the mitzvot between a person and his fellow, including the mitzva of "love your fellow as yourself," charity, helping others, doing righteous justice, and the prohibitions against lying, stealing, insulting and speaking lashon ha-ra (slander). The mitzvot connected to the family should also receive a central place, including the mitzva of marriage and its joy, fidelity in marriage, the mitzva of honoring parents, being fruitful and multiplying, and educating children.

The study should include the history of Israel as explained in the Tanakh and in the words of the Sages: from the Patriarchs, through the enslavement in Egypt, the going out to freedom, the receiving of the Torah, the entry into the Land, the period of the Judges, the Prophets and the Kings, the two Temples, the destruction and the sins that caused it, the long exile and its meaning, and up to our own day, in which we have merited the beginning of the fulfillment of the prophecies of consolation about the ingathering of the exiles and the establishment of the State of Israel, the beginning of the flowering of our redemption. Within this one should explain the central place of the Land of Israel, the mitzva of settling the Land, and the mitzva to serve in the army and defend the people and the Land. And in contrast, one should teach him about the sin of the spies and its grave consequences, up to the destruction of the Temple and the Holocaust, and the fasts that were instituted in memory of the destruction.

Likewise, one should teach the convert about Shabbat, on which Israel rests from its work and delights in the Shabbat meals in the company of family, remembers the faith in the Creator of the world, and engages in Torah; teach him about the festivals and the great ideas they express; teach him the principles of the mitzvot of kashrut and the ideas hidden in them; and teach him about prayer and blessings, without loading him with many details. The main thing is that from everything he learns, he understand how the practical mitzvot establish life on foundations of faith and morality, and how fulfilling them adds blessing to the individual, to his family, to his people and to the whole world.

In this way, the study of the mitzvot will not deter the one converting, but will strengthen his identification with the faith of Israel and its Torah, and will increase his desire to fulfill mitzvot. And even if he does not keep a religious way of life, he will fulfill many mitzvot.2

sections.title: The Declaration of Acceptance of the Mitzvot
sections.html:
After the beit din decides to accept the one converting, the custom is that he stands and declares his acceptance of Judaism and the faith, the Torah and the mitzvot. Admittedly, the Sages did not institute the recitation of this declaration; they said only that the beit din should inform the convert of some of the lighter and more stringent mitzvot, and the convert should "accept" upon himself the conversion and Judaism, without specifying how this "acceptance" is carried out. Simply understood, the "acceptance" was accomplished by the convert's very request to convert, as well as by his agreement to immerse before a beit din for the sake of entering Judaism. However, in recent generations, in order to enhance this acceptance, most conversion batei din have adopted the custom that the one converting stands and declares his acceptance of Judaism and the mitzvot. Through this declaration they also verify that the one converting understands the meaning of the conversion, and thereby ensure its validity.

Since the Sages did not establish the recitation of this declaration, it has no fixed text. In many batei din a text along these lines is said: "I accept upon myself to observe and fulfill all the mitzvot of the Torah, and all the mitzvot of the Sages, and all the proper customs of the people of Israel. And I believe in the One God. Hear, O Israel, the Lord is our God, the Lord is One."

It seems fitting to recommend this text: "I hereby accept upon myself to join the heritage of the faith of Israel, and to be a partner in its destiny to bring blessing to the world. I hereby accept upon myself to join the Jewish people and to be in brotherhood and mutual responsibility with all of Israel wherever they may be. I hereby accept upon myself, together with the whole people of Israel throughout its generations, the mitzvot of the Torah and the mitzvot of the Sages, and all the good customs of the Jewish people. Hear, O Israel, the Lord is our God, the Lord is One."

It is good that the one converting, or one of the judges, also read the word of God to Avraham our father: "And the Lord said to Avram: Go forth from your land, and from your birthplace, and from your father's house, to the land that I will show you. And I will make of you a great nation, and I will bless you and make your name great, and you shall be a blessing. And I will bless those who bless you, and the one who curses you I will curse, and in you shall all the families of the earth be blessed" (Bereishit 12:1-3). Thereby the convert will identify with the mission of Avraham our father, who was the father of converts, and with the destiny of Israel to bring blessing to the whole world.

After the conclusion of the declaration ceremony before the beit din, the conversion process must be completed by immersion in a mikveh for the sake of conversion before a beit din. Also, while the one converting is in the waters of the mikveh, one of the three judges present at his immersion asks him again about his desire to accept Judaism and the mitzvot and to convert, and after he again agrees to this, he immerses his entire body in the water, and thereby he becomes a Jew forever. When it is a woman converting, it is preferable that a woman review the acceptance of the mitzvot with her again, and the beit din listen (below 9).

Since men must undergo brit mila before the immersion, we will first explain the mitzva of circumcision, and afterward we will continue to the immersion, with which the conversion is sealed for men and women.

sections.title: Brit Mila
sections.html:
After God chose Avraham our father and commanded him to establish, together with Sarah our mother, a blessed people in the Land of Israel, they underwent many trials. After they withstood them, God revealed Himself to Avraham our father and commanded him and his descendants regarding circumcision, so that through it they would enter into a covenant with God and merit to be fruitful and multiply and to inherit the holy Land. As it is stated (Bereishit 17:1-11): "And the Lord appeared to Avram and said to him: I am God Almighty; walk before Me and be wholehearted. And I will set My covenant between Me and you, and will multiply you exceedingly … and you shall be the father of a multitude of nations … And I will establish My covenant between Me and you and your descendants after you throughout their generations, as an everlasting covenant, to be God to you and to your descendants after you. And I will give to you and to your descendants after you the land of your sojournings, all the land of Canaan, as an everlasting possession, and I will be their God … This is My covenant, which you shall keep, between Me and you and your descendants after you: every male among you shall be circumcised. And you shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between Me and you."

Brit mila expresses the destiny of the people of Israel to elevate and repair the material world as well. Many tend to think that holiness is revealed only in the heavenly spiritual world, whereas the bodily and earthly aspects express sin and evil. But the faith of Israel is the faith of unity, according to which holiness can and must be revealed in all areas of life, in heaven and on earth. Through brit mila, which is performed on the body, in the place where the strongest life force is found, holiness is drawn down from heaven to earth, and the blessing in the body is revealed. This holiness continues afterward in the mitzva of marriage and in the mitzva of settling the Land. As God promised Avraham our father, by virtue of brit mila the people of Israel will merit to be fruitful and multiply and to inherit the holy Land, which will give its blessing to all of Israel until the blessing spreads to the whole world. Since brit mila expresses Israel's faith of unity and their role in bringing blessing to the world, the Sages said (Mishna Nedarim 3:11): "Great is circumcision, for were it not for it, the Holy One, blessed be He, would not have created His world, as it is stated (Yirmeyahu 33:25): Thus says the Lord: If not for My covenant day and night, I would not have set the ordinances of heaven and earth."

Therefore, after the beit din has decided to accept the convert into Israel, the convert must, like all of Israel, enter into the covenant with God through circumcision. Care is taken to perform the brit mila before the immersion, because the brit mila may deter the convert, and therefore it is right to check first that he is indeed ready to undergo it, and only afterward complete his conversion with immersion. In addition, according to many, as long as the convert is uncircumcised, his immersion is not effective for him, and therefore he is obligated to be circumcised first, and only afterward can he immerse and convert.3

Since brit mila is part of the conversion process, it must be performed during the day and before a beit din of three, and the mohel (circumciser) is counted as one of the three (above 4, note 2). However, unlike the judges who decide on accepting the convert, who must be Torah scholars, the three before whom the brit is performed need not be Torah scholars, since they are not required to decide the question of accepting the convert, but only to be present at the time of the brit (above 4:2).

sections.title: The Order of Brit Mila for a Convert
sections.html:
The brit mila, that is, the removal of the foreskin, must be performed in the way all of Israel perform brit mila for their sons – by a Jewish mohel, a male, with intention for the sake of the mitzva. Admittedly, many hold that a Jewish woman is also fit to circumcise, since the main thing is that the circumciser be obligated in the mitzvot of the Torah; however, in practice the custom is that only a Jewish male circumcises, so that the mitzva is performed by a person who is himself obligated in brit mila (Avoda Zara 27a; SA and Rema 264:1).

When the one entering the covenant is an adult, the circumcision is more painful for him, and in order to ease the pain, the custom is to anesthetize the area of the circumcision.4

Before the brit, the mohel recites: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to circumcise converts," and immediately removes the foreskin. When the convert is not an infant, care is taken that during the blessing the area of the circumcision be covered, for a blessing is not recited in front of uncovered nakedness.

Afterward, one of those present recites over a cup of wine the blessing of Ha-gafen and another blessing: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to circumcise converts and to draw from them the blood of the covenant, for were it not for the blood of the covenant, heaven and earth would not endure, as it is stated: 'If not for My covenant day and night, I would not have set the ordinances of heaven and earth.' Blessed are You, Lord, who makes the covenant" (Shabbat 137b; SA 268:5).5

After the blessing he continues and says: "Our God and God of our fathers, sustain this man in the Torah of God and in His commandments, and let his name be called in Israel: so-and-so son of Avraham our father. May he rejoice in the Torah and exult in the mitzvot. Give thanks to the Lord, for He is good, for His kindness endures forever. May this so-and-so, son of Avraham our father, become great; just as he has entered the covenant, so may he enter into the Torah of God and His commandments and into good deeds."

Afterward, it is customary to say the verses: "Hear, O Israel, the Lord is our God, the Lord is One." "The Lord is King, the Lord was King, the Lord shall be King forever and ever." "Please, Lord, save us now; please, Lord, grant us success now."

After the convert heals from the circumcision, he immerses and completes his conversion. And although, after the decision to accept the convert, it is a mitzva to complete the conversion promptly, since there is concern that the water will infect his wound, the immersion is delayed until he heals (Yevamot 47b).

sections.title: The Mikveh and the Preparations for Immersion
sections.html:
The immersion with which the conversion is sealed for men and women is carried out by immersing the entire body at once in a mikveh of pure water (Peninei Halakha, Taharat Ha-mishpaḥa 10:1-2; 9). That is, rainwater that has collected in the ground, or spring water, or the sea; for as long as the water is collected in the ground in its natural way, it is pure, and one who immerses in it becomes pure. When the Temple stood, immersion had an important place in the order of life of all of Israel, for through it they were purified from impurity in preparation for entering the Temple and for eating pure foods. After the Temple was destroyed, most immersions lapsed; however, a kind of holiness of the Temple remained in the sanctified covenant of love between a woman and her husband, and therefore the mitzva of immersion that has remained for us is a woman's immersion for her husband after her period, in preparation for renewed union with her husband. In the immersion of converts and their joining the holiness of Israel there is also a kind of that same holiness of the Temple.

As stated, the immersion is carried out by immersing the entire body at once in the waters of the mikveh. If one immersed and left even one finger or one hair outside the water, the immersion is invalid. Nor will it help to immerse that finger or hair again; rather, one must immerse again the entire body with all the hair at once in the water. For this reason the custom is that at a woman's immersion, another woman stands and sees that all her hair enters the water (below 9).

The water alludes to the supernal kindness, through which God bestows life upon all His creatures, and when the waters are gathered together in a mikveh, they express the idea of unity that is revealed in Knesset Yisrael (the Congregation of Israel). Thus the convert who immerses in the water absorbs himself in the supernal kindness and is included in the holiness of Knesset Yisrael, and as a result, when he comes up from the water, he is as if born anew.

In addition to the requirement that the entire body be in the water at once, there must be no ḥatzitza (intervening substance) on the body or hair that would prevent the water from coming into contact with the body or hair, such as glue, paint, or discharge in the eye. This is the rule: whatever constitutes a ḥatzitza in the immersion of a nidda for her husband constitutes a ḥatzitza in the immersion of converts (Yevamot 47b; SA 268:2). Therefore, before the immersion one must wash the entire body well and shampoo the hair, in order to clean them of any ḥatzitza. To ensure that the washing removes every ḥatzitza, it should be done calmly and without pressure. A woman who has long hair must comb it well in order to undo all the knots in it. As part of the preparations for immersion, one must clean the teeth of food remnants, for although the water of the mikveh need not enter the mouth, food stuck between the teeth constitutes a ḥatzitza in the immersion. Likewise, the custom is to cut the nails in preparation for the immersion, to ensure that not a trace of dirt remains under them. Women customarily remove rings and earrings before the immersion, since under certain conditions they constitute a ḥatzitza.6

sections.title: The Order of Immersion Before the Beit Din
sections.html:
With the immersion the conversion process is completed and sealed, and from the moment the convert has immersed in the water, he is a Jew forever. Since the conversion depends on a beit din, the immersion must take place before a beit din of three men (above 4:1). Before the immersion one again verifies that the convert wishes to convert (above 5).

Immediately after the immersion the convert recites: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us concerning immersion." And although blessings are usually recited before performing the mitzva, since before the immersion the convert is not yet a Jew, the blessing is postponed until after the immersion (SA 268:2). In honor of the blessing, a male convert covers his head and places his arm under his heart, in order thereby to separate between the heart and the nakedness (for women all this is only an enhancement; see Peninei Halakha, Taharat Ha-mishpaḥa 5:6, note 3).

The immersion of a female convert must also be before three judges. In order to preserve modesty, the female convert wears a loose garment under which the water enters, so that it does not form a barrier between her body and the water of the mikveh. In addition, a woman accompanies the female convert in the mikveh, and only after the female convert is in the water does she call the three judges, who stand at a distance, in such a way that they see only the head of the woman converting; and from there one of the judges asks her about her desire to join the people of Israel and the covenant with God, and about her desire to accept the mitzvot. It seems that if possible, it is preferable that the woman accompanying the female convert ask her about this, and the judges listen. Afterward the woman converting immerses, the judges see her head go under the water, and the woman with her verifies that all her hair is in the water and that the immersion is valid. With this the conversion is complete and the judges leave. The blessing over the immersion need not take place in the presence of the judges (see below, halakha 13, whether in pressing circumstances one may immerse not before the judges).

A female convert who was pregnant at the time of the conversion – her immersion is effective also for the child who will be born to her, and therefore there is no need to immerse him for conversion after he is born (SA 268:6). And since he is Jewish from birth, he is circumcised on the eighth day even if it falls on Shabbat7

sections.title: Welcoming the Convert After the Immersion and Holding a Celebration
sections.html:
After the immersion, the judges and those accompanying welcome the male or female convert with words of honor and love. As the Sages said: "When he has immersed and come up, we say to him good words, words of comfort: To whom have you attached yourself? Fortunate are you! To the One who spoke and the world came into being, blessed be He, for the world was created only for the sake of Israel, and none are called children of the Omnipresent but Israel, and none are beloved before the Omnipresent but Israel!" And the judges, who at first challenged him with questions and appeared to be rejecting him, say to him: "All those things that we said to you, we said only in order to increase your reward" (Tractate Gerim 1:1).

It is a beautiful custom to bless those converting by reciting a "Mi She-berakh," like the blessing recited for those called up to the Torah, or in a personal wording. It is especially good to say a "Mi She-berakh" for a female convert, since within the blessing she is called by the Jewish name she has chosen for herself, and thereby her name is established with a blessing: "May He who blessed our fathers Avraham, Yitzḥak and Ya'akov, and Sarah, Rivka, Raḥel and Leah, bless so-and-so (her Jewish name) daughter of Sarah our mother. May the Lord reward your deeds, and may your reward be complete from the Lord, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge. May the Lord fulfill all the wishes of your heart for good, and save you from every trouble and distress, and from every affliction and illness, and send blessing and success in all the work of your hands, and let us say Amen" (a male convert is called by his Jewish name after the brit mila, above, halakha 7).

It is fitting for the convert to recite Sheheḥeyanu for having merited to join the people of Israel.8

It is fitting to hold a se'udat mitzva (festive meal) with relatives and friends after the immersion, in honor of the completion of the conversion. If they did not manage to hold a celebration on the day of the immersion, it is fitting to hold a celebration in the following days, for it is fitting to mark the entry into the covenant with God with festivity and joy.

sections.title: Marriage and Waiting Three Months
sections.html:
A gentile couple who converted must marry according to the law of Moshe and Israel after their conversion, and without this they are not considered married. At the ḥuppa all the blessings of betrothal and marriage are recited, and likewise the Sheva Berakhot (seven blessings) are recited at the end of the wedding meal held on the wedding day.9

The Sages instituted that before the marriage they must separate from each other for three months, so that if a child is born to them, it will be possible to distinguish whether he was conceived in the holiness of Israel after the conversion, or not in holiness before the conversion. On rare occasions this knowledge also has halakhic importance, for if another son is later born to them, and he marries and dies without children, the law is that if the first son was conceived in holiness, he must perform yibum (levirate marriage) with his brother's wife or perform ḥalitza for her; and if he was conceived not in holiness, his brother's wife is exempt from yibum or ḥalitza, for halakhically he is not considered his brother, and consequently he is also forbidden to perform yibum with her (Yevamot 42a; SA EH 13:5; YD 269:9).

If at the time of the conversion it was known that the female convert was pregnant, they need not separate, since it is known that the conception was not in holiness (Masoret Ha-giyur 15:9). For the same reason, if the female convert has reached the stage at which she can no longer give birth, they need not separate (Dagul Me-revava EH 13:5; Masoret Ha-giyur 15:11).

If after the conversion the female convert had her period, since one can thereby know with certainty that she did not begin a pregnancy before the conversion, she may marry immediately afterward without waiting three months (Igrot Moshe EH 2:5). Similarly, nowadays a pregnancy test can be performed, and whenever she has taken a test and it has become clear with certainty whether or not she began a pregnancy before the conversion, she may marry immediately without waiting three months, and this is the practice (see Masoret Ha-giyur 15:12).10

sections.title: The Law of a Convert Who Was Circumcised Before His Conversion
sections.html:
A convert whose foreskin was removed while he was still a gentile, not for the sake of Judaism, must have hatafat dam brit (drawing a drop of covenantal blood) performed on him. That is, just as is done for a Jewish infant who was born without a foreskin, from whom covenantal blood must be drawn, so the mohel makes a light scratch on the one converting at the place where the foreskin was attached, in order to draw out a drop of blood from there, and thereby the convert enters the covenant. According to many, a blessing must be recited over the drawing of the blood; however, since some hold that there is no obligation to draw covenantal blood from one who has no foreskin, no blessing is recited (SA 268:1).11

The son of a Jewish father and a gentile mother, who was given a brit mila in the way Jews customarily do, and who as an adult comes to convert, does not need to have covenantal blood drawn again. And although at the time of the brit they did not intend thereby to begin the process of his conversion, since they performed the brit for the sake of the mitzva in the way of all Israel, he thereby entered the covenant of Avraham our father. Admittedly, some hold that since they did not perform the brit for the sake of conversion, covenantal blood must be drawn from him for the sake of conversion. And although the main ruling follows the view of the overwhelming majority of the poskim, who do not require drawing blood, if the convert so wishes, it is good to draw covenantal blood from him.12

A convert who underwent brit mila but retracted his intention to convert, and after some years returned and asked to complete his conversion, does not need to have covenantal blood drawn again; and if the beit din sees that he is worthy of conversion, he completes his conversion with immersion alone (Minḥat Ḥinukh, mitzva 2, 23).

One who cannot be circumcised because his organ was severed converts like a woman, through immersion alone, without brit mila. But one who has a foreskin and cannot be circumcised because of danger cannot be converted.13

Although we have learned that the conversion is completed only through circumcision and immersion, already after the circumcision the convert is considered as one who has begun to enter the covenant, for he is circumcised like a Jew.14

sections.title: Immersion of a Female Convert Not Before a Beit Din
sections.html:
As we have learned (above 4:1), the immersion for conversion must take place before a beit din of three, and when the immersion took place not in the presence of a beit din, the Rishonim disagree whether it is effective. This law became a practical matter in places where female converts could not immerse before a beit din of three, and then the question arose whether, after the fact, a conversion can be carried out without the beit din being present at the immersion. In the year 5653 (1893), a need arose to convert gentile women in Melbourne, Australia, but there was no mikveh for women there. Most of the Jewish women there did not immerse for their nidda in a valid immersion but bathed in a bathtub, and only a few righteous women were careful to immerse at the seashore designated for women's bathing. Since, according to the accepted standards of modesty, the rabbis could not come to the seashore to see the immersion of the female converts, Rav Avraham Hirschowitz sent a question to the Rav of Jerusalem, Rav Shmuel Salant, about how to proceed. Rav Salant answered that, there being no alternative, one should instruct that three Torah scholars go with the female convert as far as it is possible to accompany her, and upright women accompany her to the seashore, and she should immerse before them according to halakha for her conversion (Responsa Beit Avraham p. 47; Rav Reinowitz answered him there likewise).

Similarly, a question arose in the large Jewish community of Salonika in Greece, in which there was no special mikveh for women; rather, the women used to immerse for their nidda in a pool fit to serve as a mikveh, which was in a bathhouse shared by gentile and Jewish women. The question was how the female converts would immerse there, when the rabbis could not enter the women's bathhouse. The Rishon Le-Tziyon, Rav Uziel, who at that time served as the Rav of Salonika, ruled to rely on the many Rishonim who hold that the immersion is valid after the fact even without the presence of a beit din. And he added that it is good that the women who go with her be agents of the beit din (Mishpetei Uziel vol. 1, YD 13).

However, when there is no such necessity, care is taken that the immersion be in the presence of a beit din of three men. In order to preserve modesty, the female convert wears a loose garment, and the judges stand at a distance and see only her head at the time of the immersion, as explained above in halakha 9.15

sections.title: The Convert's Sacrifice
sections.html:
As we have learned (above 1), conversion is carried out in the manner of Israel's entry into the covenant with God, which also included the offering of sacrifices. First Israel offered the Pesaḥ sacrifice on the night of the plague of the firstborn, and thereby expressed their faith in God and their rejection of the idols of Egypt (Mekhilta de-Rabbi Yishmael). Afterward, at Mount Sinai, they offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, and the ceremony of their consent to accept the Torah was accompanied by the sprinkling of the blood of the sacrifices upon Israel, in order thereby to express their absolute closeness to God. As it is stated (Shemot 24:3-8): "And Moshe came and told the people all the words of the Lord and all the ordinances, and all the people answered with one voice and said: All the words that the Lord has spoken we will do. And Moshe wrote all the words of the Lord, and rose up early in the morning, and built an altar at the foot of the mountain, and twelve pillars for the twelve tribes of Israel. And he sent the young men of the Children of Israel (the firstborn, who then served as priests), and they offered burnt offerings and sacrificed peace offerings of oxen to the Lord. And Moshe took half of the blood and put it in basins, and half of the blood he dashed against the altar. And he took the book of the covenant and read it in the hearing of the people, and they said: All that the Lord has spoken we will do and we will hear. And Moshe took the blood and sprinkled it on the people, and said: Behold the blood of the covenant which the Lord has made with you concerning all these words."

Correspondingly, when the Temple stood, in order to complete his conversion, the convert offered as a burnt offering two turtledoves or two young pigeons, or an animal (Keritot 8b).

When there is no possibility of bringing sacrifices, the convert converts without offering a sacrifice, for it is a principle that in all generations it is possible to convert, as it is stated (Bamidbar 15:14): "And if a stranger sojourns with you, or whoever is among you throughout your generations." For it is impossible that a matter as great as conversion should be nullified in any generation; rather, it is necessary that whenever there is a person who wishes to convert, it will be possible to accept him. Therefore, in a generation in which there is no possibility of offering sacrifices, the convert converts without a sacrifice, and when the Temple is rebuilt the convert will bring his sacrifice (Rambam, Issurei Bi'ah 13:5).16
It can be said that when the Temple stands, the convert must express his closeness to God through a sacrifice, for the sprinkling of the sacrifice's blood on the altar expresses the convert's desire to draw close to God with self-sacrifice. But when the Temple is destroyed, the Shekhina is not revealed in Israel in its full splendor, and Israel is in danger from its enemies, and the sacrifice that Israel must constantly offer is their self-sacrifice for their faith in God and for preserving their identity and their mission to bring blessing and repair to the world. And when a convert wishes to join the people of Israel at a time when the Temple is destroyed, he too is ready to offer this great sacrifice for the sake of repairing the world.
